sentences: A young man leans on a window ledge and blows a soap bubble.
It has just swollen into shape, and its thin, translucent skin catches the sunlight in shimmering colours.
This is Soap Bubbles by the French painter Jean Siméon Chardin.
It is painted in oil on canvas, 61 centimetres high and 63.
2 centimetres wide, almost a perfect square.
It is dated to around 1733 or 1734, and it belongs to The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.
Look first at the bubble.
A single breath, begun at a glass of soapy water, has become a clear sphere floating out beyond the ledge.
Because we know it will burst at any moment, we find ourselves holding our breath too.
Now look down along the ledge.
A small child peers eagerly over it, eyes fixed on the bubble.
The child is curious, but silent, and the hush of concentration that fills the picture is not broken.
Look at the young man's jacket and hair, his forehead and his hands.
Chardin lays on the paint in a way that looks rough yet is finely judged, bringing out the weave of the cloth and the warmth of skin.
It was these astonishing surface effects that made him famous.
In earlier Northern European painting, soap bubbles carried a moral message about the brevity of life: our days, like bubbles, vanish in an instant.
Chardin does not preach.
He shifts the subject from allegory to everyday life, turning it into a moment of the ordinary game that everyone has played.
Chardin was born in Paris in 1699 and died there in 1779.
Although he was a member of the Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture throughout his career, he did not study at the Academy and had little traditional training in drawing from the model.
This picture is counted among the works from the years when he first turned seriously to the human figure.
He made his own copies of his most successful compositions.
Later versions of Soap Bubbles belong to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art and to the National Gallery of Art in Washington, and the Met's canvas is known as the earliest of them.
The painting also has a painful history.
It was seized by the Nazis from the collector Jane Mannheimer in Paris and illegally purchased in 1944 for Hitler's planned Führer Museum.
After the war it was returned to France and restituted in or after 1948, and the Met acquired it in 1949.
Today it hangs in gallery 629 of The Met Fifth Avenue, and the museum has recorded its own audio guide track for it, so you can stand in front of the bubble and listen.
Step back and take it in: a bubble about to burst, a young man holding his breath, a child looking up.
Think of a moment today that you watched to the very end, even though you knew it would not last.
